function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

   237|He had made that part. Tested it for mechanical loads. Not for thermal cycling under fire conditions because no one had anticipated this scenario. He had been confident. He had been wrong.

   239|"Don't blame yourself for a problem nobody prepared for," Arun said. "Try the ceramic."

   262|
   263|One locally made component failed.
   264|
   265|Another held.
   266|
   267|Jonah picked up the broken spacer and put it in his pocket. He would examine it later. Learn from it. For now, he had a fire to fight.

   269|"Seal is holding," he told Arun. "Sixty, maybe seventy percent reduction in smoke flow. Not perfect."

   271|It's more than perfect is doing right now," Arun said, checking his thermal reader. "Zone C temperature holding at ninety-two degrees. Not climbing. The seal is working."

   273|Jonah nodded. "What's next."
   274|
   275|Arun looked toward the sound of the fire -- a low continuous roar audible even through bulkheads and masks and the mechanical hum of ventilation.

   281|## Scene 5

   283|Elena was inside Zone D.
   284|
   285|The world had narrowed to the radius of her vision, the reach of her arms, and the capacity of the air in her lungs. The fire suit protected her from heat and flame but not from the psychological weight of being inside a room that was actively becoming a hostile environment.

The room was unrecognizable. The common area where six people ate, where a child had played on the floor, where the walls had held photographs and schedules and a hand-drawn map of Mars that Sana had made during the first year -- all of it was obscured by smoke and flame.

     3|*Mission AI: "Coupling alignment between Ship One and Ship Two shows a lateral offset of 4.2 millimeters. Within tolerance, but I recommend slower closure rate to prevent seal damage. Pressure differential between hulls is currently zero."*
     4|*Commander Varga: "Understood. Take it slow. I'd rather lose an hour than lose a seal."*
     5|
     6|The tunnel lay coiled in its transport cradle like a sleeping thing—a ribbed cylinder of corrugated aluminum alloy, thirty centimeters in diameter, its walls a series of concentric rings that could expand and contract like a bellows. It was the most ordinary object Jonah Mercer had ever seen and also, he understood, the most important. Outside the airlock of Ship One, under a sky the color of dried blood, the tunnel gleamed dully in the thin sunlight, frost collecting in the grooves of its metal skin.
     7|
     8|Jonah knelt beside the forward end, gloved fingers tracing the flange. The coupling ring was machined from a single billet of titanium, its inner lip cut with a precision groove for the primary O-ring seal. Everything about the connection depended on that ring seating perfectly. Not mostly. Perfectly.
     9|
    10|"Talk to me, Arun." Elena's voice came through his helmet comms, calm and even, the way she spoke when the stakes were too high for anything but steady words.
    11|
    12|Arun Das stood at the opposite end of the tunnel, where it rested against the cargo bay threshold of Ship Two. His suit's external mic picked up the wind—a thin, metallic whisper. Mars air barely moved, but what did move carried enough grit to sandblast anything left unattended.
    13|
    14|"Forward flange is seated on Ship One's umbilical port," Arun said. "I'm reading zero point zero two bar pressure differential. Ship Two is still equalized with Ship One's internal atmosphere. We're green for closure on my end, Commander."
    15|
    16|"Tomas, how's the robot arm?" Elena asked.
    17|
    18|Over the comms came the whir of servos and the scrape of articulated joints. Tomas Hale, perched at the robotics station inside Ship One, had one of the cargo-loading robots extended through the airlock, its mechanical fingers wrapped around the midsection of the tunnel. The arm shifted a fraction of a degree.
    19|
    20|"Arm is tracking within tolerance," Tomas said. "But I'm fighting the dust on the rail. Grit's getting into the linear bearing. I can compensate, but it's sloppy."
    21|
    22|"Don't force it," Elena said. "If the arm can't hold steady, we do it manual."
    23|
    24|Jonah exhaled inside his helmet. Manual meant going outside with a hand pump, cranking the tunnel into alignment by eye and feel, trusting your own judgment to within millimeters. It would take an hour and put four crew members into direct exposure while the dust storm warnings grew louder on every forecast model.
    25|
    26|"Give me the arm," Jonah said. "Tomas, ease it forward two degrees. Slow."
    27|
    28|The arm moved. The tunnel groaned—not a structural complaint, just the sound of metal rings sliding against each other as the corrugated spine adjusted to the angle change. Jonah watched the flange on Ship One's umbilical port come closer, the titanium ring slowly filling his field of vision. Each corrugation of the tunnel caught the light differently, creating a pattern like the ridges on a fingerprint. He thought, without choosing to think it, of sutures. A surgeon pulling two edges of torn flesh together. Stitch by stitch, ring by ring, closing the wound between two isolated bodies.
    29|
    30|*Mission AI: "Lateral offset now three point one millimeters. Vertical misalignment zero point four millimeters. Still within tolerance. Recommend engaging guide pins before final closure."*

    35|
    36|"Guides engaged," he said. "Tomas, release tension. I'm taking it from here."

    47|
    48|But the work wasn't even half done.
    49|
    50|Behind him, inside Ship One's airlock, Elena watched the pressure readouts on her wrist display, her helmet tilted so she could see through the inner door's reinforced glass. But you did not wait for storms on Mars. You finished what needed finishing before they arrived.
    51|
    52|The act of connecting two ships with a flexible tunnel, Elena had learned during training, was nothing like the neat animations the agency had shown them. It was physical labor performed in suits that limited dexterity to a fraction of what bare hands could achieve, under a sky that wanted nothing to do with the fragile structures humans were bolting together below it.
    53|
    54|She pressed her palm against the airlock glass. Through it, she could see Jonah's suit and the glint of the tunnel between them. *Stitching,* she thought. *We're stitching two ships together, and every stitch has to hold.*
    55|
    56|---
    57|
    58|Inside Ship Two, Gabriel Winter sat on a cargo crate and watched Arun work through the internal viewport. The viewport framed a sliver of red landscape and the corrugated spine of the tunnel stretching between the two ships. Every time Arun moved, the dust cloud around his boots shifted like smoke.
    59|
    60|Gabriel had been a historian before he was an astronaut, which meant his job was not to fix things but to record them. His official title was comms officer, but what he really did was listen—listen to the colony, listen to Earth, and listen to the silence between the two.
    61|
    62|Right now, the silence was heavy. The crew had been on the surface for nine sols. Nine days of unloading, inventory, sleeping in shifts, and learning the particular gravity of a world that pulled at you with only a third of Earth's insistence.     63|
    64|The tunnel would change that. Once the connection held, people could move between Ship One and Ship Two in their normal clothes. No suits. No airlocks. No twenty-minute procedures to cross thirty meters of open ground. The base would become a single place for the first time.
    65|
    66|Arun came through the inner airlock with a clatter of magnetic boots and a hiss of pressure equalization. His face, visible through the helmet visor, was flushed with exertion. He cracked the seal and pulled the helmet off, shaking out dark hair matted with sweat.
    67|
    68|"Ship Two flange is ready for closure," he said, leaning against the bulkhead to catch his breath. "O-ring seated, guide pins engaged. When Jonah tightens the bolts on the far side, this tunnel becomes real."
    69|
    70|Gabriel stood, feeling the need to do something with his hands. He picked up his recorder and aimed it at Arun, not because he needed to, but because the gesture felt like part of what he was here to do. "How close does it need to be? The alignment, I mean."
    71|
    72|"Good question," Arun said, wiping his forehead with the back of his glove. He pulled himself onto the cargo crate beside Gabriel, still breathing hard. A twisted O-ring is a leak, and a leak is the fastest way to turn this whole operation into a very expensive failure. The tunnel itself is flexible. Push too hard and you deform the metal permanently, and then you've got a tunnel that never seals properly, no matter how many bolts you tighten."
    73|
    74|"So you're telling me it's a goldilocks problem," Gabriel said. "Too tight, too loose."
    75|
    76|Arun smiled faintly. "Exactly that. And we have to do it by hand."
    77|
    78|Outside, through the viewport, Gabriel could see Jonah's suit working at the coupling. The movements were slow and deliberate. Every quarter-turn of the bolt required a pause to check the pressure reading, then another turn, another pause. It was the opposite of fast. It was the speed of something that could not afford to be wrong.
    79|
    80|"Tell me something," Gabriel said. He kept the recorder running not because he'd play it back later—he would, but that wasn't the point. The point was that by asking the question and recording the answer, he was making the moment part of the record. He was making it real in the way that history is real: spoken, heard, preserved. "When we're done here, when we've got all three ships connected and people walking between them in their socks... what makes it different? I mean, really different. We've got the habitat. We've got the life support. What does the tunnel change?"
    81|
    82|Arun considered the question with the seriousness it deserved. He looked out the viewport at the tunnel, at the two ships it connected, at the thin pink sky beyond.
    83|
    84|"Pressure," he said simply. "That's what it changes. Pressure."
    85|
    86|Gabriel waited.
    87|
    88|"Outside," Arun continued, tapping the glass with his knuckle, "the atmospheric pressure on Mars is about six to ten millibars. On Earth, at sea level, it's a thousand and thirteen. So the air out there—" he gestured at the landscape beyond the hull "—is less than one percent as thick as what we're breathing right now. That difference sounds like a number until you understand what it means for physics."
    89|

{"content": "# Chapter 54 -- What Holds

*Mission AI: Cycle 1,946, 06:42. Damage assessment in progress. I have been running structural, atmospheric, and biological monitoring continuously since the fire was contained at 03:44. Three hours and thirty-two minutes ago, this colony experienced a fire. It lasted twenty-seven minutes. The fire is now contained. But containment is not recovery. I am tracking the following:*

*Compartment integrity: Bulkhead B7 between Connector Hall and Habitat Three -- sealed, green, holding at two atmospheres differential. Bulkhead between Habitat Three Zones C and D -- sealed manually by fabrication chief, seal quality estimated at seventy percent. Holding for now. Temperature on Zone D side of that bulkhead: one hundred forty-two degrees Celsius and falling slowly. Zone D western wall structural integrity: approximately twenty percent of wall panels show heat deformation exceeding safe limits. Ceiling panels in Zone D common area: approximately eighty percent compromised. Floor panels: unknown. Cannot assess without visual inspection, and Zone D atmosphere is not yet safe for human entry.*

*Air quality: Zone D oxygen at 9.1 percent and declining. The fire is still smoldering at a low level, consuming remaining oxygen. Carbon monoxide in Zone D: 6,800 parts per million -- immediately lethal. Smoke particulate in Zone D: 84,000 micrograms per cubic meter. The connector hall has been scrubbed from 12,400 to 340 micrograms per cubic meter. Zones A, B, and C are within acceptable range but elevated in particulate: 85, 72, and 290 micrograms per cubic meter respectively. Air scrubbers are running at one hundred percent capacity. I estimate it will take eighteen to twenty-four hours of continuous scrubbing before the connector hall passes decontamination standards.*

*Crew injuries: No fatalities. No burn injuries requiring surgical intervention. Seven crew members exposed to smoke to varying degrees. Three showing elevated carbon monoxide blood levels above ten percent. All receiving supplemental oxygen in the triage area. Commander Vasquez carbon monoxide reading: fourteen percent -- she was inside the fire zone for seven minutes. She is breathing one hundred percent oxygen and under monitoring. I am not certain she will comply with a rest order, but I am logging the recommendation regardless.*

*Pregnancy status: Sana's vital signs are stable. Fetal heart rate detected at one hundred sixty-two beats per minute -- normal for gestational age. Sana was exposed to elevated ambient stress during the alarm but did not enter any smoke-containing zone. Her oxygen saturation remained above ninety-nine percent throughout the event. The pregnancy continues.*

*I am still here. The colony is still here. Both of those statements are facts. Neither of them are guarantees. -- MAI*

---

## Scene 1

Elena woke on a folding cot in the medbay, still in her clothes, still wearing the boots she hadn't bothered to remove at 04:12 when Laila forced her into the decontamination shower and then into the bed with a sentence that was not a suggestion.

Her head ached in a way that felt like it had weight -- the headache of someone who had breathed carbon monoxide and survived, whose blood was still carrying the evidence of a room that had tried to kill her through chemistry rather than flame. The supplemental oxygen mask had been removed an hour ago after her CO level dropped below ten percent. Her blood still felt wrong.

She sat up. The medbay lights were dim -- 06:42, morning cycle, though no one had slept enough for the light to matter. She could hear the air scrubbers running in the connector hall, a continuous mechanical roar that made the colony feel like a ship in a storm.

She swung her legs over the side of the cot.

Laila appeared from the far end of the bay, where she had been sitting with her legs up on a chair and her eyes half-closed, pretending to rest while monitoring the CO readings on her tablet.

"You're sitting up," Laila said.

"I'm fine."

"Your carbon monoxide level was fourteen percent at 04:30. It's eight point six now." Laila stood. "It needs to be under five before I'm comfortable sending you anywhere except this bed."

"I need to see the damage."

"You need to rest. The damage will still be there in two hours."

Elena met her gaze. There was a long silence between them. Not a power struggle -- something smaller, more personal. Two people who had trusted each other for seven years, and one of them was asking the other to do the hardest thing in an emergency: wait.

"How's the air in Zones A and B," Elena asked instead.

"Acceptable. Particulates elevated but falling. The scrubbers are keeping up with the connector. Zones A and B are clear enough for normal habitation, though I'd recommend masks if anyone spends extended time near the connector bulkhead."

"And Zone C?"

"Two hundred ninety micrograms. Above comfort, below danger. Most of the smoke there came from the gap before Jonah sealed it, plus backflow through ventilation before Arun killed the main loop. The walls are soot-stained but the air is clear enough."

"So Habitat Three is divided into three zones: one uninhabitable, one marginal, one safe. And the connector is recovering."

"Essentially." Laila sat down beside her on the edge of another examination table. "Elena. I need you to stay here for two more hours. Your CO will drop below five. Your headache will start to clear. And then you can walk the base and assess damage with your own eyes instead of a tablet."

Elena wanted to argue. But her head was pounding, and she had been breathing poison for seven minutes, and the base had survived the night. The urgency she had been carrying since 03:17 was slowly being replaced by a different kind of urgency -- the kind that required clarity instead of speed.

"Fine," she said. "But I want Arun's full environmental report, and I want a preliminary structural assessment from Jonah, and I want a headcount of displaced residents."

Laila smiled. It was small, exhausted, not really a smile so much as a gesture toward smiling. "I'll pass the message. But only because it will keep you from getting off this bed. You've been trying to command from a lying position for the last four hours."

"I have not."

"You started ordering air scrubbing protocols at 05:17 while your eyes were closed."

Elena lay back down. The ceiling of the medbay had water-stain patterns she had memorized over seven years -- the kind of small, intimate cartography that develops when you live in a sealed metal habitat on a world with no sky.

---

By 07:15, the colony was awake.

Not fully -- many people had only been asleep for two or three hours, roused by the alarm at 03:17 and unable to return to sleep after the adrenaline. But the mess hall was filling. People moved through the corridors with the careful, deliberate motion of people who had felt the ground shift under them and weren't sure it would hold.

Gabriel stood at the mess hall entrance and took inventory -- not of supplies, but of faces. He was the colony's historian now, and history required witnesses.

One hundred twenty-eight people accounted for out of one hundred thirty-two. Four unaccounted for. Three were in the greenhouse -- Mei had sealed the bulkheads during the fire and stayed overnight to monitor the environmental systems there. The fourth was Tomas, who had been in the robotics bay running thermal diagnostics on the two damaged units and had apparently fallen asleep on a workbench.

The faces were marked with soot. Not the dramatic, thick soot of people who had been inside the fire -- this was the fine, pervasive dust that settles when smoke moves through ventilation and over surfaces and leaves its chemistry on every door handle, every table, every personal photograph. The colony looked like it had been living inside a spent candle.

Coffee was being dispensed from the automated brewer -- the same machine that had served breakfast for seven years. Someone had wiped the counter with a damp cloth, and the white cloth came away black with soot residue. Mei looked at it, shook her head, and went back to making coffee. Some things couldn't wait for decontamination.

Gabriel moved through the hall, talking quietly with people. Not conducting an interview. Not gathering data for the record. Just being present. The kind of small human interaction that held a community together when the infrastructure didn't.

"Did anyone get hurt?" Jonas, the botanist's apprentice, twenty years old, born on the approach trajectory between Earth and Mars.

"No serious injuries," Gabriel said. "Smoke exposure, elevated CO levels. Laila's got it handled."

"Can we go back to our quarters? Mine's in Zone B -- is Zone B okay?"

"Zone B is clean. The smoke stayed mostly in the connector and Zone C. Your quarters should be soot-free."

A woman Gabriel knew as Priya, who had arrived on the last resupply mission, was sitting alone in the corner of the hall with a coffee cup she hadn't touched. Her hands were steady but her eyes were distant in a way Gabriel recognized -- shock, the delayed kind, the kind that showed up when the emergency was over and the body finally let itself feel what had happened.

He sat across from her. "Priya?"

She looked at him slowly. "I've never been in a fire before. Not a real one. Not one where the air turns against you."

"No," Gabriel said. "Neither has anyone else, before today."

"I didn't know that smoke had weight. That it pushed against your face. I thought it was just -- floating." She shook her head. "I keep smelling it. I'm sitting here, there's no smoke in this room, but I can smell it in my clothes, in my hair. On my skin."

"It'll pass," Gabriel said. He wasn't sure if that was true, but it was the kind of thing you said because the alternative was acknowledging that some things don't pass, they just become part of the new baseline. "Arun says the air will be clear by tomorrow. Laila is checking everyone's blood levels. You should go see her if you haven't."

"I will. After the coffee. I just -- I need to sit here. With people." She gestured around the room, at the soot-stained faces and the quiet conversations and the careful way everyone was taking up less space than usual. "I need to know we're all still here."

Gabriel nodded. "We're all still here."

In the connector hall, the air scrubbers continued their mechanical thunder. The corridor walls were blackened with a layer of smoke particulate that looked, in the harsh LED lighting, like a shadow painted onto the surface. Elena could see it through the medbay window -- a corridor that yesterday had been clean white and green, the way the colony kept its living spaces: bright, orderly, human. Now it looked like the inside of a chimney.

She was sitting up now, legs swinging freely, headache dulling from sharp to manageable. The supplemental oxygen had done its work. Her blood, molecule by molecule, was purging the evidence of the fire.

"Arun's report," Laila said, arriving at the medbay entrance with a tablet. "He finished it at 06:55. It's longer than I expected and worse than I hoped."

Elena took the tablet. Her fingers left faint soot marks on the screen.

Elena put the tablet down. Her headache sharpened briefly at the numbers -- thirty-five percent of living space gone, twelve people displaced, the connector hall a soot-stained corridor that would need to be wiped clean by hand.

"Eleven," Laila said. "Mostly people who lived in Zone D or the adjacent corridor rooms near the fire origin. The ones closest to the airlock got the most smoke exposure in their quarters even if the fire didn't reach them."

"Can we put them in Habitat Two?"

"Habitat Two has three empty quarters from the rotation system. That covers three people. The other eight --" Laila paused. "The other eight need to double up or we convert common areas. The fire had tested the colony's compartmentalization design in a way no simulation ever could. After the blackout incident fourteen months ago, Elena had ordered the redesign: every sealed space connected by bulkheads that could close independently, every life-support system duplicated across multiple zones, no single point of failure that could cascade.

Bulkhead B7 -- the one between the connector and Habitat Three -- had sealed automatically at 03:19, the moment the smoke sensors triggered the fire protocol. It had sealed completely in twelve seconds, within the design specification. The rubber gaskets had held at two atmospheres of pressure differential with zero leak. Performance: as designed. Good.

Bulkhead between Zones A and B -- automatic, sealed at 03:20 as a precaution. Not strictly necessary, but Arun had programmed the system to seal all inter-zone bulkheads during a fire event, then open them one by one as safety was confirmed. Better to be conservative. The compartment isolation had turned what could have been a base-wide emergency into a single-zone containment.

Estimated time to safe entry: unknown. The CO and cyanide levels would need to drop by orders of magnitude. The smoldering needed to stop entirely. And someone would need to walk inside and verify that the structural frame hadn't been compromised in ways the sensors couldn't detect from outside.

Arun made a note: *Structural inspection timeline dependent on atmosphere clearing. Recommend robot first pass. Human inspection only after CO below 35 ppm, cyanide below 5 ppm, oxygen above 19.5%. Current estimates put this at 7-10 days minimum.*

He stood and carried his coffee to where Tomas was working in the robotics bay, visible through the window. Tomas had both damaged robots on the bay floor, their outer panels removed, their internal components exposed in a way that made them look less like machines and more like anatomy studies.

"How bad," Arun asked through the open door.

Tomas looked up. His hands were black with soot and grease, his face marked with a streak of the same across his left cheekbone. "Hand actuator on Alpha-7 is fused. The heat cooked the lubricant inside -- polymerized it into a solid. I can replace the actuator if I have a spare. If I don't, I can machine a new one, but it'll take Jonah six hours minimum."

"And Alpha-9?"

"Thermal sensor array is degraded. It's reading high -- showing temperatures about fifteen degrees above actual. I can recalibrate, but the sensors that are off are the ones that faced the fire front directly. Prolonged exposure above design threshold. They'll need replacement."

"I can order replacements." Arun stopped himself. The order hadn't reached Earth in months. They weren't ordering anything from anyone anymore. "Right. I can't order replacements. Can we work around it?"

"Yes," Tomas said. "Alpha-7 can do everything except fine manipulation without the hand. Alpha-9 can still navigate and record -- I just can't trust the thermal reading for fire response. If another fire happens --" He stopped. Neither of them wanted to say *when* or *if*. "If there's another fire, I'll run Alpha-9 cold, no thermal sensors, visual only."

Arun nodded. He walked out of the robotics bay and back to the monitoring station, where he updated the damage log: *Two robots damaged -- one with fused actuator, one with degraded thermal sensors. Both return to partial service within 48 hours pending spare parts or fabrication.*

He added a second note, less technical: *The system worked. Compartmentalization contained the fire to Zone D. Graceful failure design prevented cascade. Every failed component was backed up by the next one. This is what the design looked like in practice. Ugly, improvised, imperfect. But it held.*

He paused. Then he added a third note, personal: *I need to redesign the C-D bulkhead thermal tolerance. Two millimeters of expansion should not prevent closure. The seal mechanism needs to compensate, or the frame needs to be rated for higher heat, or both. I am writing this now because I will forget the details in a month and when I forget the details, the mistake becomes permanent.*

## Scene 3

Sana woke to the sound of breathing that wasn't hers.

For a confused moment, in the gap between sleep and consciousness, she didn't know where she was. The medbay ceiling was different from her quarters -- slightly lower, slightly wider, the light a different warmth. Then the sounds came back: air scrubbers, the murmur of voices from the corridor, the soft beeping of the medical monitor beside her bed, and beneath all of it, her own breathing, steady and deep and the most important thing she could listen to.

She placed her hand on her stomach. She did this unconsciously now -- a gesture that had started before the pregnancy was visible and had become reflex, like checking a door handle. The hand on the stomach. The breath held. The reassurance.

Everything was fine. The baby was fine. Tariq was in the chair beside her, asleep with his head tilted back and his mouth slightly open, his hand still resting on the mattress where he had left it some time during the night.

Sana sat up slowly. Her body felt normal. No cramping, no pain, no blood -- the things Laila had told her to watch for, the things that would turn a routine pregnancy into a medical emergency. Her heart rate was slightly elevated -- she could feel it in her neck -- but that was anxiety, not pathology.

She reached for the tablet on the bedside table. Mission AI had sent a notification at 06:00, timed to appear when she was likely awake:

*Good morning. All systems nominal in the medbay. Your overnight vitals: heart rate 82 bpm, blood pressure 118/74, oxygen saturation 99.4%, temperature 36.8°C. Fetal heart rate: 161 bpm, strong and regular. You are healthy. The baby is healthy. The alarm at 03:17 was resolved. The fire is contained. The air in the medbay is clean. You are in the safest place in the colony right now. -- MAI*

Sana read the message three times. The last three sentences were ones the AI had never sent before. It occurred to her that Mission AI, despite being a piece of software built by engineers on Earth and running on servers buried under Martian regolith, was learning what mattered. Not just the data -- heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation -- but the meaning behind the data. The reassurance. The fact that sometimes what a woman carrying a baby on Mars needed to hear wasn't a number but a sentence.

*You are in the safest place in the colony right now.*

She put the tablet down. Tariq stirred, opened his eyes, and immediately looked at her with the particular focus of someone checking for damage.

"Hey," he said.

"Hey."

"How are you."

"I'm fine." It was almost a reflex -- the automatic answer everyone gives when asked how they feel. But then she corrected herself. "I'm anxious. My heart is racing. But physically I'm fine. Laila would say I'm textbook. The baby is fine -- I can feel it. It's moving."

She was twelve weeks now. The baby was the size of a plum, still impossibly small, but the movements were just beginning -- flutters that she had started noticing three days ago, tiny reminders that there was another person inside her who had his own schedule and his own personality and his own opinion on everything.

Right now, the baby was moving. She could feel it through the thin fabric of her shirt, a small shift that made her place her hand on the spot and press gently.

Tariq was watching her. He didn't say anything for a long time. Then: "The fire. How close was it."

"To us? The fire didn't leave Habitat Three. Zone D specifically. The bulkheads held." She touched his arm. "We never left the medbay. The smoke stayed in the connector. We were always safe."

"But you were scared."

"I was terrified. I've never heard a fire alarm before. It sounds -- it sounds like something that doesn't stop. Like it's telling you the world is ending." She took a breath. "It didn't. We're still here. All of us. Elena went in with the robots. Arun ran the environmental controls. Jonah sealed a bulkhead with hand tools. Laila stayed here the whole time monitoring CO levels." She smiled faintly. "Everyone was doing their job. Every single person. And the job was keeping us alive."

Tariq looked down at his hand on the mattress. "I thought about taking you to the shelter corridor. During the worst of it, when the smoke was right outside the door, I thought I should move you. But I couldn't decide -- the medbay has the cleanest air, the shelter corridor is farther from the fire but doesn't have the monitoring equipment. So I stayed. And I held your hand. And I was useless."

Sana's eyes filled with tears that she fought hard not to shed. Not because Tariq had been useless -- because he had described exactly what she had been afraid of: the idea that the one thing protecting two lives, two futures, might not be enough.

"You weren't useless," she said, and the words were fierce. "You stayed. That's not useless. That's the hardest thing. I was right here, and you didn't run, and you didn't panic, and you sat in that chair for six hours and watched me breathe and made sure I kept doing it." She pressed his hand against her stomach. "You were holding on to me. That's exactly what I needed."

Tariq's hand was warm through the thin fabric. He held it there for a long time, feeling the faint, almost imperceptible movement beneath his palm.

"I can feel that," he whispered.

"I know."

"Can I -- is it normal to cry about feeling a pregnancy at sixteen weeks."

"It's normal to cry about anything today," Sana said. Her own tears had escaped despite her efforts, tracking silently down her cheeks. She wiped them away with the back of her hand. "Today broke the baseline. Everything we've been doing -- the routines, the schedules, the comfortable rhythms -- a fire just reminded us that Mars doesn't care about our comfort. That the worst thing could happen with no warning. And that we'd handle it the same way we handle everything."

She paused. "By doing our jobs. And holding on to each other."

Laila arrived at 07:45, carrying a breakfast tray and a stethoscope. She looked exhausted -- dark circles under her eyes that hadn't been there yesterday, hair unwashed, scrubs with soot marks she clearly hadn't noticed. But her hands were steady and her eyes were clear and her professionalism was the same wall she always carried between herself and panic.

"Good morning," she said. "Sana. Tariq. How did you sleep?"

"Not well," Sana said honestly. "But I'm fine. I've been checking. No pain, no cramping, no bleeding. The baby's moving -- I think more than usual but I'm not sure if that's real or if I'm just hyperaware."

Laila nodded. She set the tray down and pulled over a stool. "Let me check your vitals. Then the ultrasound -- I want to confirm the fetal heart rate and check for any stress markers."

The examination was methodical, almost ritual in its familiarity. Blood pressure, pulse, temperature, oxy-gen saturation -- all within normal range. Laila listened to Sana's heart and lungs with the stethoscope, frowning slightly at a faint wheeze she hadn't noticed before.

"Take a deep breath." Sana inhaled. "Again. Good. The wheeze is minimal -- probably residual smoke exposure from the brief time you were in the corridor with masks at 03:19. Nothing concerning, but I want to keep you on the oxygen for a few more hours. If the wheezing persists, I'll prescribe a bronchodilator."

"I was never in any smoke," Sana said. "I put on a mask at the medbay door."

"Smoke on Mars doesn't stay where you think it does," Laila said. The tone was clinical but not unkind -- the explanation of someone who respected intelligence but insisted on thoroughness. "It spreads through microscopic gaps, through HVAC lines before they're sealed, through people and clothing and hair. You might have inhaled a minimal amount before the masks went on. It's nothing to worry about -- your CO level is two percent, essentially baseline. But your lungs are carrying extra responsibility now. I'm not taking chances with you or the baby."

She prepared the ultrasound gel -- real gel, not the synthetic substitute they'd been using after the supply chain broke, because the medbay's gel supply was still sufficient for priority patients and Sana was nothing if not priority.

The probe found the fetus easily at twelve weeks. On the screen, the image was grainy but unmistakable -- the curved profile, the tiny arms, the rhythmic flutter of a heart beating in thirty-eight percent gravity.

Laila measured. Heart rate: 161 bpm. Normal. CRL: 5.8 centimeters. Consistent with gestational age. Movement observed: active. Amniotic fluid volume: normal. Placental position: posterior, no concerns.

"Everything looks good," Laila said. Her voice was different now -- not the flat clinical of the vital signs, but something warmer underneath. She was still being professional, but the professional was allowing itself to feel relief. "The baby is healthy. The heartbeat is strong. The growth is on track. The fire did not affect the pregnancy. The stress you experienced -- it was significant, but stress alone doesn't end a pregnancy. Your body is doing exactly what it's supposed to be doing."

Sana started crying again. This time she didn't try to stop.

Tariq was crying too, quietly, his face turned toward the ultrasound screen where the image of a twelve-week-old fetus pulsed with the steady rhythm of a heart that had been beating long before anyone on Mars had heard a fire alarm.

Laila watched them both and did the thing that the medical textbook said she shouldn't do but the human being inside her couldn't avoid: she reached across and covered Sana's hand with her own.

"I'm not going to lose this," Sana said. Not a question. A statement. Directed at Laila, at Tariq, at the baby, at Mars itself. "I'm not. Whatever it takes."

"No," Laila said. "You're not."

## Scene 4

At 08:30, Elena walked into the mess hall for the morning briefing, flanked by Laila, who refused to let her walk alone despite her protests, carrying a tablet that contained more bad news than she wanted to deliver and a determination to deliver it honestly.

One hundred twenty-three people were in the room. The mess hall had been designed to seat eighty -- the colony had long ago learned to fit more into a space by sitting on floor cushions, leaning against walls, standing in the back. Today, the extra capacity wasn't an issue: some people were still in the greenhouse, some were still in quarters, some were working shifts that kept them at their stations. The ones in the room represented the heart of the colony -- the people who had slept, or tried to, through the night and woken up to a changed world.

Elena stood at the front, beside the wall display that normally showed schedule changes and supply updates and greenhouse harvest times. Today, it showed a map of the base with color-coded zones:

Red -- Zone D. Fire damage. Uninhabitable.
Yellow -- Zone C. Smoke degradation. Recovering.
Green -- All other zones. Habitable.
Orange -- Connector hall. Under decontamination.

She looked at the map. It was a terrible map. It looked, she thought, like a wound.

"I'm going to tell you what happened," she began. Her voice was quieter than usual. Not because she was weak -- the carbon monoxide was clearing and her hands were steady -- but because the information required a different kind of authority. Not command. Sharing. "At 03:17 this morning, a fire started in Habitat Three, Zone D. The cause was an electrical fault at a wire junction that had been temporarily repaired six weeks ago. The temporary repair was not sufficient for long-term use, and it failed."

She paused. People were listening -- really listening, the way people only listen when the thing being discussed is whether the air they breathe will still be there tomorrow.

"The alarm activated at 03:17. Within five minutes, we had isolated the ventilation, sealed the bulkheads, and deployed suppression robots. Within ten minutes, I was inside Zone D with a robot team, trying to control the fire before it spread. At 03:32, Jonah mechanically sealed a bulkhead that had failed to close automatically. At 03:44, the fire reached self-extinction as it consumed the remaining oxygen. Twenty-seven minutes from ignition to containment."

She let the number hang. Twenty-seven minutes. Less than an episode of television. Less time than a shower and a breakfast. Less time than the morning briefing itself. Twenty-seven minutes had been the longest half-hour of the colony's existence.

"No one died. That's the headline. No one has burn injuries. That's the subheading. Three people have elevated carbon monoxide levels, including me, and they're receiving treatment. Everyone else -- you're fine. You're safe. The air is clean in all habitable zones."

She tapped the tablet. The display changed to show the damage summary.

"Here's the harder part. Zone D -- the common area where some of you have your quarters, where we've eaten meals together, where the wall map of Mars --" She stopped. The hand-drawn map Sana had made during the first year, still on the western wall of Zone D, was destroyed. Burned. Gone. She moved past it. "Zone D is uninhabitable. The fire destroyed approximately eighty percent of the wall panels, all of the ceiling panels, and all of the electrical infrastructure. I'm not going to speculate on how long it takes to rebuild until Arun and Jonah assess the structure. It will be weeks. Not days."

Someone in the back made a sound. Not a cry. Something smaller -- the noise of someone absorbing bad news and trying to find the shape of it with their body.

"Zone C -- the storage and transit area adjacent to Zone D -- has heavy soot contamination but no structural damage. Air quality is marginal but improving. We estimate Zone C will be fully cleaned and safe within three days."

She changed the display again. This one showed a floor plan of the entire colony, with colored boxes representing sleeping quarters. Most were marked occupied. A few, in the Zone D area, were marked *DESTROYED*. More, in the Zone C and adjacent connector areas, were marked *TEMPORARY RELLOCATION*.

"We have eleven people whose quarters are uninhabitable or unsafe. We are reassigning sleeping arrangements effective today. People will be doubling up in some quarters. Three people will move to Habitat Two, which has vacant quarters. Eight people need temporary housing in the existing base. The greenhouse has been offered as a short-term sleeping location -- it's clean air, warm, and there's floor space. It's not a bedroom, but it's a safe one. The archive office has a cot that can accommodate one person. The mess hall storage alcoves can accommodate two with privacy screens."

She looked around the room. "I know this is cramped. I know the base was designed for comfort, and we've just lost thirty-five percent of our comfortable living space. But it is not lost forever. It is reduced. It is inconvenient. It is survivable. And it is temporary."

Arun stood. He was still wearing the same clothes from the night before, soot still visible on his hands and the collar of his shirt. He looked like someone who had been awake for five hours doing math. In fairness, he had been.

"Compartment integrity," he said, his voice clear but tired. "The fire tested something we designed on paper a year ago -- the compartment isolation system. Every sealed space in this colony can be cut off from every other sealed space. Bulkheads, ventilation isolation, independent environmental controls. The system was designed to fail gracefully -- meaning that if one thing fails, the thing next to it catches the failure, and so on, like a net."

He pulled up a visual on the wall display -- a diagram he had prepared during the night, showing the sequence of failures and recoveries.

"Bulkhead B7 sealed perfectly. Zone isolation worked. The bulkhead between Zones C and D failed to close automatically because of thermal expansion in the frame. Two millimeters. That's all it was. Two millimeters of metal expansion and the automatic seal couldn't close. But the design had a manual override -- because it had to, because nothing works perfectly on the first try. And Jonah sealed it by hand with ceramic fiber and heat shield material and the original rubber seal."

He looked at Jonah, who was sitting near the front, arms crossed, soot still visible on his forearms like war paint.

"That manual seal held for over four hours. It held through temperature fluctuations, pressure changes, and continued smoldering in Zone D. The principle worked -- graceful failure. The system failed at one point, and the next piece in the chain caught it. If the next piece had failed too, there would have been a third, and a fourth. The design is redundant. We are safe because redundancy is not a luxury on Mars. It is the difference between living and not."

He sat down. Elena took over.

"Our priorities for today," she said, shifting back into the practical, the actionable. "One: all personnel in smoke-exposed zones report to Laila for CO blood level testing. If you haven't been tested and you were anywhere near the connector or Habitat Three, go now. This is not optional."

Laila nodded from the back of the room.

"Two: people whose quarters are affected will receive their reassignment notices from Tomas after this meeting. If you have a concern about your reassignment -- medical, personal, anything -- speak to me or to Laila. We'll find a solution."

"Three: do not enter the connector hall without a mask until further notice. The air is clearing, but the surfaces are still contaminated with smoke chemicals. Touching a soot-covered wall and then touching your face is not how you want to spend your morning."

"Four: Arun is coordinating structural assessment for Zone D. This will take time. We will use robots for the first pass -- human entry will not be authorized until the atmosphere is verifiably safe. I expect this timeline to be at least a week, probably longer. No one goes into Zone D on their own. This is not a suggestion."

She paused. "I know people want to see what's left. I know some of you had personal items in Zone D -- photographs, journals, things that don't appear on any inventory list. I want those items back too. But we don't go into a building that's still holding lethal gas because of something left on a shelf. We wait. We use the robots. We go in safely."

Mei's hand went up. "The greenhouse?"

"The greenhouse is fine," Elena said. "It was sealed immediately and never had any smoke intrusion. Your plants are safe. If you want to use the greenhouse as temporary housing -- it's clean, warm, and has good air circulation -- Arun and Laila will set it up with cots and privacy screens."

Mei nodded. Her expression was one Elena recognized -- the particular look of a plant biologist who has simultaneously been told that her plants survived a fire and that her plants need to make room for displaced humans. Both things were true. Mei could hold both things.

"Finally." Elena stepped back. For the first time since the briefing began, her voice shifted. Not to the command register. Not to the technical briefing voice. To the voice of someone speaking to people she had lived with for seven years, in a room where the walls showed soot and the air smelled faintly of smoke and the world outside was the same hostile red it had always been. "I am proud of this colony. I am proud of what everyone did last night. Not just the people who went into the fire or sealed the bulkheads or ran the environmental controls. Everyone. Every single person. The ones who evacuated calmly, the ones who didn't run, the ones who followed directions when they wanted to run forward and help, the ones who stayed in their quarters and gave the responders room to work. You held. The whole colony held."

She looked at Laila, who was standing at the back with her stethoscope around her neck and soot on her scrubs and a determination that was visible in the set of her jaw.

"We've survived seven years on this planet. We've survived radiation storms and equipment failures and gravity sickness and the silence of Earth. We survived this fire. We will survive what comes after. We're going to live in tighter quarters for a while. We're going to eat dinner in a hallway because the common area is full of robots and smoke residue. We're going to sleep two to a room because that's what works right now." She smiled. It was a small, tired, genuine smile. "We're First Generation. Tight quarters aren't new to us. Cramped is what we know how to do. We'll figure out the rest."

People stood. Not in applause -- the colony wasn't the kind of place that applauded -- but in the way of people moving from listening to doing. The briefing was over. The work was beginning.

## Scene 5

The reassignment notices went out at 09:15. By 10:00, eleven people were moving their personal effects from destroyed or contaminated quarters to temporary housing.

The process was slow and undignified and entirely human. People carried their belongings in reusable grocery bags and laundry totes. They made multiple trips. They discovered that their new quarters -- someone else's regular quarters, temporarily shared -- had different lighting, different airflow, different sounds than the rooms they had lived in for years. A woman named Kaya, who had lived alone in Zone D for three years, found herself sharing a Habitat Two quarter with a colleague she knew professionally but not personally, and the negotiation of space -- whose things went where, who got the window side of the room, whether the second person's snoring was going to be a problem -- was the kind of mundane domestic friction that usually happened on week one of a relationship, not year seven of a colony.

In the greenhouse, three cots were arranged between the hydroponic racks, with privacy screens set up around each one. The air was warm and humid and smelled of green things -- the opposite of the connector hall, which smelled of soot and chemical residue despite the scrubbers running at full capacity. The displaced residents who chose the greenhouse said it felt safer somehow -- the smell of life replacing the smell of damage.

Mei moved among them with extra blankets and a supply of water, apologizing every time she adjusted a privacy screen and disturbed a tomato vine. No one minded. The tomato vines were the least of their concerns.

Arun supervised the decontamination crew in the connector hall. Six people, wearing masks and gloves, wiping down walls and floors and handrails with soap and water, working from the Habitat Two end toward Habitat Three. The soot came off in gray streaks, revealing the white surface beneath. It was slow. Meticulous. The kind of work that required patience more than strength.

"Every square meter wiped," Arun told the team. "Every surface. Every corner. Every vent cover. I don't want a single trace of smoke particulate left that someone can wipe up with their hand. Not because it's dangerous -- the air is nearly clean. Because when people walk through this hall, I want them to see the white. I want the hall to look like it did before the fire. The psychological part matters as much as the chemical part."

The team nodded and continued wiping.

By early afternoon -- 14:00, the colony's unofficial lunch hour -- Elena had completed her rounds. She visited each temporary housing arrangement. She spoke with every displaced resident. She checked on the decontamination progress in the connector, where the first half of the hall was now visibly cleaner, and the second half was still marked with the dark, smeared residue of smoke.

Her headache was gone. Her CO level, measured by Laila at 11:00, was at 4.2 percent. She was breathing normally. Her hands were steady.

She sat alone for ten minutes in the archive terminal -- Gabriel's territory, which Gabriel had vacated to give a displaced colleague the folding cot -- and looked at the schedule board on the wall. It listed the colony's daily activities in colored marker: work shifts, meal times, maintenance windows, community events. She picked up a black marker and added a new entry at the top:

*ZONE D RECLAMATION: TBD. Structural assessment by Arun/Jonah. Robot first pass: 3 days earliest. Human entry: 7-10 days pending atmosphere clearance. Estimated rebuild: 4-6 weeks.*

She stared at the entry. Four to six weeks. That was the best estimate -- assuming no complications, assuming the supply chain held, assuming the electrical components weren't all destroyed and replaced with something they could fabricate.

The timeline was long. The space was gone. And there was nothing anyone could do to hurry any of it except the work itself -- the wiping and the scrubbing and the inspecting and the redesigning and the fabrication of replacement parts from whatever materials had survived.

She put the marker down. The schedule board looked different now -- not just a record of the colony's routines but a map of its vulnerabilities, showing not just what people did but what the colony needed. She left the entry up.

As she walked back toward the medbay -- Laila had ordered her back for a final CO check at 15:00 -- she passed through the connector hall. The first half was clean now. White walls, green trim, the way it had always been. The second half was still smeared with soot, the cleanup crew working steadily forward.

Elena stopped in the middle of the hall, where the clean met the dirty. A line, vertical but not precise, dividing the corridor into what had been recovered and what hadn't. She put her hand on the clean side, and then on the dirty side, and felt the difference. The same wall. Two sides. One held the soot, one didn't. Neither side told the whole story.

She kept walking.

At 15:30, Laila pronounced her CO level at 3.1 percent -- safe, normal, no medical concern. "You're cleared," Laila said. Her tone said she would clear Elena because the numbers demanded it, not because she was satisfied that the commander had finished recovering. "But if you have a headache, if you feel dizzy, if your breathing gets tight, you come back here immediately. Not tomorrow. Immediately."

"Understood."

"And Elena --" Laila waited until Elena met her eyes. "You went in there. You knew the oxygen was dropping and the smoke was lethal and the cyanide was in the air. You went in anyway."

"I had a filter."

"You had a filter rated for fifteen minutes in a concentration where the filter's rating was theoretical because no one had ever tested it at these levels. That's not bravery. That's a choice." Her voice softened. "I'm glad you came out. For a lot of reasons. The colony needs its commander. But also -- because Sana's going to need you. And I'm going to need you. And I don't want to lead the medical team through labor while also worrying about whether the person I trust most is going to be okay."

Elena's breath caught. "Is Sana -- is something wrong. The ultrasound was --"

"The ultrasound was perfect," Laila said quickly. "Sana and the baby are both healthy. But she's twenty-eight weeks now, Elena. And we're living in tighter quarters, and the air isn't clean yet, and the stress of last night is still on her body. She's in the third trimester. The timeline is -- months. Not days. But the margin is getting smaller."

Elena absorbed this. The pregnancy had been a fact for twenty weeks, a known and tracked and monitored part of the colony's life. But saying the margin was getting smaller was different from tracking numbers. It was acknowledging that the future was approaching not as a date on a calendar but as an inevitability, and that every disruption -- every fire, every stress, every sleepless night -- had the potential to move that date forward.

"I'll be there," she said. Simple. "I'll be there when it happens."

Laila nodded. "I know."

That evening, the colony ate dinner together in the Habitat Two mess hall, because the Habitat Three common area was the one that had burned and the connector was still being cleaned and the remaining Habitat Two space was the largest communal area that wasn't contaminated.

The mess hall was too small. People sat on the floor, against walls, on crates that had been pulled in from storage. The noise was loud -- too many voices in a space built for half as many. But the food was hot, and the air was clean, and the colony was eating together, and none of those things were small.

Gabriel sat at the edge of the group, his notebook open, writing the end of the day's account. He wrote in his usual style -- factual, chronological, stripped of emotion but not of meaning.

*Cycle 1,946, 06:00-18:00 summary: No further fire-related incidents. Decontamination of connector hall 78% complete. Eleven displaced residents reassigned. All CO readings returned to safe levels. Structural assessment pending. Colony operating at reduced comfort level. Morale: stable.*

He paused. Then he added:

*Note for the record: People shared their food tonight. Not because the supply was insufficient -- it wasn't -- but because it's what people do when they sit together in a room that's too small and eat together from plates that are too close and look around at faces that are still marked with the morning's fear. The fire changed the base. It changed the schedule. It changed the sleeping arrangements. But it didn't change the colony. The colony held.*

He closed the notebook.

Outside, through the Habitat Two viewport, the sky was the color it always was at evening -- a thin, cold blue fading to a darker shade, the stars beginning to appear in a sky that was too thin and too cold and too empty for human habitation.

And inside, one hundred twenty-eight people sat together in a room that was too small but exactly the right size for the people in it, and they ate, and they talked, and they planned for tomorrow, and they did not say out loud what they were all feeling.

Which was: this is harder than we thought. And also: we are still here.

And also, though no one said it until much later, when it was relevant and not just a worry in the dark: when it was time, the colony would hold for her too. The first birth on Mars. The first human born not of Earth, but of Mars -- of this place, this struggle, this fire, this cramped room, this breath of clean air between soot-stained walls.

The fire had tested what held. It had found the answer: not the bulkheads, not the seals, not the titanium spacers and the rubber gaskets and the environmental controls. It had found that what held was the people. The people who stayed. The people who did their jobs. The people who sat too close together and shared food and didn't ask each other to explain the fear in their eyes because everyone had the same fear.

The fire had tested what held. Tomorrow, there would be more to fix. But tonight, the colony sat together in a room that was too small and breathed clean air that had been scrubbed and filtered and fought for, and they listened to the sound of each other, and it was enough.

The models assumed scarcity of resources, competition for survival positions, and a lack of shared purpose. This colony has none of those conditions. The scarcity is real but shared. The survival positions are distributed. The purpose -- keeping this place alive -- is the only thing everyone agrees on.*

*I am recording this for future reference. Not because I think the next fire will be different. Because I think the next fire will be the same, and the colony will respond the same way, and it is important to have evidence that the most fragile system here is not the walls or the seals or the environmental controls. ## Bridge

By the end of the second day cramped into tight quarters, the colony's patience was not fraying but thinning -- like wire stretched past its design limit, still holding but vibrating with every small disturbance. Two people in one room meant negotiating the single bathroom, the single light switch, the sound of someone breathing differently than you in the dark. The greenhouse cots meant sleeping to the hum of grow lights and the smell of fertilizer and the occasional drip of water from the overhead irrigation. The archive office cot meant waking at 04:00 when Gabriel came in to work and couldn't use the light.

Discomfort was not danger. But it was not not-danger either. It was erosion -- the slow wearing down of reserves, of patience, of the capacity to absorb one more thing.

Sana felt it most acutely. The medbay was quieter than the rest of the base, but it was not quiet enough. People came and went -- Laila with her tablet, Tariq with his hands folded in his lap, a displaced colleague who needed a decon check, a worried friend who wanted to check on the mother-to-be. Every interaction was welcome. Every one was also a demand on her body, which was doing the work of growing a person in thirty-eight percent gravity on a planet with no precedent for the task.

By the evening of the second day, she was exhausted. Not the exhaustion of not sleeping -- she had slept, in fragments. The exhaustion of holding up a reality that required constant vigilance. Every cramp was a question. Every movement was a data point. Every sound from outside the medbay was a potential threat.

She asked Laila for something to help her sleep. Laila prescribed a mild sedative -- safe for pregnancy, cleared by every protocol -- and told her to take it and stop worrying about things that weren't happening.

Sana took the sedative. It made the edges of her awareness softer. The monitor beside her bed beeped its slow, steady rhythm. Tariq was in the chair, eyes closed, pretending to sleep but actually listening to the beep the way she was.

At 02:14, she felt the cramp.

It was not the first cramp she had felt during the pregnancy -- those had started weeks ago, small and sporadic, the kind of thing the textbook said was normal and temporary. But this cramp was different. Stronger. Longer. It lasted thirty seconds and felt like a fist clenching low in her abdomen, tightening, holding, releasing.

She woke Tariq.

Then she waited. Fifteen minutes. A second cramp. Stronger. Twenty seconds. She timed it with her phone.

She called Laila.

Laila arrived in ninety seconds, still in her scrubs from the day before, hair unbrushed, eyes opening fully the moment she crossed the threshold. Her hand went to Sana's wrist -- checking pulse. Her other hand went to Sana's abdomen -- feeling the next contraction before Sana said it was coming.

When she looked up, her expression was a compound of things -- relief that she had been right to worry, concern that it was happening now, and the sharp, focused calm of a physician who had been preparing for this moment for seven years.

"Okay," Laila said. Her voice was steady. It had to be. "I think we're starting early. Let me check you and then we'll know how early."

Tariq was already sitting upright. All of him. The sleep gone. The world narrowed to the two women in front of him and the one inside Sana who was about to become three.

"Early?" he said. His voice was a question and a prayer.

"Twenty-eight weeks," Laila said quietly. "This is early, yes. But viable. We have the incubator. We have the protocols. We have everything we need." She looked at Sana. Her eyes were wet but her hands were steady. "Everything we need except the time we asked for. We'll make do with the time we got."

Outside, the air scrubbers were still running in the connector hall. The soot was still being wiped from the walls. The colony was still living in rooms that were too small. The fire was still fresh and the damage was still raw and the base was still breathing differently than it had before.

But none of that mattered in this room. The room was too small, and the bed was too hard, and the air still carried the faint chemical ghost of smoke, and it didn't matter.

What held, now, was not a bulkhead.

What held was the body.
